result.summary: Jove sends a lying Dream to Agamemnon, who tests the army by proposing flight; the men rush for the ships until Minerva and Ulysses restore order, and Ulysses beats Thersites. The Achaeans feast, arm and march out, and the poet lists the Achaean and Trojan contingents.

scenes.title: Jove sends the lying Dream
scenes.summary: Jove sends a Dream in Nestor's likeness to tell Agamemnon he will take Troy. Agamemnon believes it.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon is deceived into hoping for quick victory, while the Achaeans face heavy slaughter.

place.name: Tent of Agamemnon at the ships

scenes.title: Council of the elders
scenes.summary: Agamemnon calls the elders to Nestor's ship, tells his dream and plans to test the army. Nestor backs him.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon risks the army truly fleeing if the test goes wrong.

scenes.title: Agamemnon tests the army
scenes.summary: The host assembles and Agamemnon, holding his ancestral sceptre, urges flight home. The men run to launch the ships.
scenes.stakes: The army may abandon the war and Agamemnon's glory.

place.name: Assembly on the shore before Troy

scenes.title: Minerva and Ulysses stop the flight
scenes.summary: Juno sends Minerva, who rouses Ulysses. He turns the men back, soothing chiefs and beating commoners.
scenes.stakes: Greek shame and defeat if the ships are launched.

scenes.title: Thersites is beaten
scenes.summary: Thersites abuses Agamemnon and urges departure. Ulysses thrashes him and the people laugh.
scenes.stakes: Thersites risks punishment for insulting the king.

place.name: Assembly on the shore before Troy

scenes.title: Ulysses addresses the assembly
scenes.summary: Ulysses, with Minerva as herald, asks patience after nine years.
scenes.stakes: The army's resolve and the Greeks' honour.

place.name: Assembly on the shore before Troy

scenes.title: The omen at Aulis
scenes.summary: Ulysses recalls the serpent eating nine sparrows, which Calchas read as nine years of war and victory in the tenth.

scenes.title: Nestor's advice and the feast
scenes.summary: Nestor urges order by tribes. Agamemnon sacrifices to Jove, who refuses his prayer. The army arms and marches, driven on by Minerva.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon risks his army's lives, with Jove's refusal ahead.

scenes.title: Catalogue of the Achaeans
scenes.summary: The poet invokes the Muses and lists the Achaean contingents, their leaders and ships, with the absent Achilles.

place.name: Greek lands and the Achaean camp

scenes.title: Iris warns Troy; Trojan catalogue
scenes.summary: Iris in Polites' likeness warns the Trojans. Hector arms them, and the Trojan allied contingents are listed.
scenes.stakes: Troy faces the advancing Achaean host.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses' defence of single rule: one king, many cannot be masters.
Invocation to the Muses before the Catalogue of Ships.

analysis.text: Jove's deceit and Agamemnon's test show how divine will and human folly shape the war, and Ulysses' persuasion restores order.
The Catalogue of Ships preserves a geography of Greek regions and tribes, possibly reflecting old Bronze Age traditions.

legacy.text: The Catalogue of Ships became the model for later epic catalogues, such as in Virgil's Aeneid.
Thersites became a byword for a scurrilous railer, and Shakespeare used him in Troilus and Cressida (c. 1602).

fun_facts.text: The Catalogue of Ships lists about 29 contingents and around 1,186 ships.

language_notes.text: "Destroyed much people" is archaic grammar: it means Jove planned to have many people destroyed. The "people" are the Achaeans, whose losses will make them miss Achilles.
Juno (the Greek Hera) sided with the Greeks against Troy. Her change of mind refers to the gods' earlier disagreement over the war.
"Dock his sleep" means cut short or reduce his sleep.
"Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, like "Achaeans"; both are used for the whole Greek army.
"Sallied forth" means set out energetically; "imperishable staff" refers to the sceptre, which Agamemnon inherited from his father Atreus.
"Wended her way" means made her way; "herald" means announce; "criers" are official heralds who summoned assemblies.
"Dock his sleep" means cut short his sleep; "son of Atreus" is Agamemnon's patronymic.
"Woe betides" means misfortune will befall. Juno (the Greek Hera) favours the Greeks and hates Troy.
"Sound them" means test their feelings; Agamemnon plans to propose flight to see whether the army still wants to fight.
"Argives" is another name for the Greeks, used alongside Achaeans.
"Wildfire Rumour" is Homer's Ossa, personified Rumour, sent by Jove to spur the crowd on to the assembly.
"Slayer of Argus" refers to Mercury killing the hundred-eyed giant Argus, set to guard Io; a standard epithet of the god.
Agamemnon's odd arithmetic: if each Trojan householder served wine to a ten-man Greek company, many companies would lack a cup-bearer, showing the Greeks' great superiority in numbers.
"Nine of Jove's years" means nine full years of the siege, measured by the god's reckoning.
The Icarian Sea is the part of the Aegean near the island of Icaria, known for rough water.
"Welkin" is an archaic word for the sky or heavens.
The "stays" are the props or supports holding the beached ships upright; removing them lets the ships slide down to the sea.
"Aegis-bearing" refers to Jove's aegis, a magical goat-skin shield or cloak that spread terror; here it is an epithet of Jove.
"Argives" and "Achaeans" are both names for the Greeks; Homer uses them interchangeably.
"Peer of Jove in counsel" means equal to Jove in wisdom and planning.
"Whereon" means "upon which," i.e. after which.
Agamemnon had tested the army by falsely proposing to go home; "sounding us" means testing our resolve, and the men took him literally.
"Sirrah" is an old contemptuous form of address for an inferior.
"Monger of sedition" means a dealer or peddler in rebellion: someone who constantly stirs up discontent against authority.
"Most wont to wrangle" means most accustomed to quarrel with them.
"Stew in his own meeds of honour" is sarcasm: let Agamemnon be left to enjoy his prizes (meeds means rewards) alone.
"Chide" means to scold or quarrel; Ulysses says Thersites has no supporters to back such defiance of princes.
"Gibe" means to jeer or taunt. "Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans and Argives.
"Prating" means chattering foolishly or at tiresome length.
"A by-word" means an object of mockery or scorn; the army's desertion would make Agamemnon a disgrace in everyone's talk.
"Restive" means restless and unwilling to be controlled; here the troops are growing impatient and unruly.
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen, offered to the gods.
"Prodigy" means a marvel or portent, here a supernatural sign sent by the gods.
"Made him become a sign" means Jove turned the serpent into a lasting sign by changing it to stone.
Oaths were sealed with drink-offerings (wine poured out) and clasped right hands; Nestor reminds the army of the solemn pledges to take Troy.
Lightning on the right was a favourable omen; Nestor recalls Jove's sign at the fleet's departure for Troy.
"Bootless" means useless or without profit; the wranglings bring no good.
"Whet" means to sharpen; "livelong" means the whole length of the day.
Barley-meal was sprinkled on the victim before slaughter as part of the sacrificial ritual.
Thigh-bones wrapped in fat were the portion burned for the gods; the people ate the rest.
The aegis is Minerva's (Athena's) divine shield or breastplate, here fringed with golden tassels and inspiring terror and courage.
Cayster is a river in Asia Minor (Lydia) near Ephesus, famous for its water-birds.
Danaans is one of Homer's names for the Greeks, along with Achaeans and Argives.
"Aegis-bearing" refers to Jove's aegis, a divine shield or goatskin cape, which was a mark of his power.
"Had lain with her" is a euphemism for sexual union; Mars (Greek Ares) fathered the two sons secretly.
Linen breastplate: light armour, unlike the bronze worn by most heroes, showing he fought lightly and relied on skill.
"Wearing their hair long behind" describes the Abantes, who let their hair grow at the back and, in some traditions, cut it in front.
Erechtheus, an early king of Athens, was said to be born from the earth and raised by Minerva (Greek Athena).
Thamyris was a Thracian singer who challenged the Muses to a contest and was punished by them.
The Arcadians lived inland and had no ships, so Agamemnon supplied them.
"Large of stature" means tall and big-bodied; heroes are often praised for size.
"Came up under Ilius" means came to Troy (Ilius is Ilium, Troy). "Danaans" is another name for the Greeks.
"Marshal" means to organize and lead troops into battle order; here the Myrmidons sit idle without a commander.
Tearing the cheeks was a traditional gesture of mourning by women. The unfinished house shows how suddenly his life was cut off.
Philoctetes was abandoned on Lemnos after a snake bite left a foul, painful wound. The Greeks later needed him to win.
Orcus and the Styx belong to the underworld; the river's oily, unmixing flow marks it as sacred, tied to oaths.
"Sons of Atreus" means Agamemnon and Menelaus, the two chief Greek kings.
Typhoeus was a monster Jove struck down with thunderbolts and buried beneath the earth; his rumbling was said to cause quakes.
"Sally" means a sudden attack made from a position; here the Trojans fear a Greek assault on the city.
"Divers" means various or several; the allies speak many different languages.
Contrasts the human name Batieia with the gods' name for the mound; Homer often notes names used by gods versus men.
A breastplate "of linen" was layered linen stiffened as armor, not cloth clothing.
"Fleet descendant of Aeacus" is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus; his killing of Trojans in the river refers to events later in the poem.
Refers to Achilles' later slaying of Nastes in the river and taking his gold, an event narrated in Book 21.

context_notes.text: Achilles has withdrawn from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon. Jove promised Thetis that he would honour Achilles by making the Greeks suffer without him.
Nestor is the oldest and most respected Achaean counsellor, so Agamemnon would trust his word.
Nestor is the aged, respected king of Pylos, known for wisdom and long experience; the elders form Agamemnon's council.
In the preceding scene Jove sent a false Dream disguised as Nestor, chosen because Agamemnon would trust him.
Nestor accepts the dream because of Agamemnon's rank as commander, not because of any proof the dream was true.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) was the smith god, so the sceptre is a divine craft object and a mark of legitimate rule.
The sceptre's descent through Pelops, Atreus and Thyestes traces Agamemnon's royal house, whose history was full of family strife.
Agamemnon is deliberately testing the army; only he and a few leaders know that his call to go home is not sincere.
Juno (the Greek Hera) favours the Greeks and hates Troy. Helen's abduction by Paris caused the war.
Olympus was the mountain home of the gods; Minerva (the Greek Athene) is goddess of wisdom and war.
Ithaca was Ulysses' island kingdom. The staff is Agamemnon's sceptre, symbol of royal authority, which gives Ulysses' orders weight.
Achilles is the greatest Greek warrior. He is at odds with Agamemnon over the seizure of his prize, the captive woman Briseis.
Telemachus is Ulysses' young son, left at home in Ithaca. Ulysses swears by his own fatherhood and his head.
The sceptre was a staff of royal authority, passed to speakers in the assembly, so Ulysses strikes with the symbol of rule.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) often aids Ulysses, who is known for cunning and persuasive speech. Here she disguises herself as a herald to quiet the crowd.
Aulis was the Boeotian harbour where the Greek fleet gathered and was held back by winds before sailing to Troy.
Calchas was the army's seer, who interpreted omens and signs from the gods.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, is the Achaeans' wisest counsellor; "Gerene" is a place epithet associated with him.
Agamemnon and Achilles quarrelled over Briseis, the captive girl Agamemnon took from Achilles; Achilles now withholds his help.
The two Ajaxes are the great Ajax of Salamis and the lesser Ajax of Locris; the son of Tydeus is Diomed.
Epic poets traditionally begin big set pieces by invoking the Muses, goddesses of memory and song, who were thought to know the past.
Ajax son of Oileus, the Locrian, is a different man from the great Ajax son of Telamon, who comes from Salamis.
Agamemnon of Mycenae is the supreme commander of the Greek army, and brings more ships than any other leader.
Menelaus, Helen's husband, is the injured party whose wife's abduction by Paris started the war.
Ulysses (Greek Odysseus) rules Ithaca and the nearby islands; he is renowned for cunning counsel.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war. Calling a hero his peer praises his fighting skill.
Hercules (the Greek Heracles) was the greatest hero of Greek legend, so his descendants were prominent.
Achilles will rejoin the fighting after Patroclus is killed, as the poem later tells.
Aesculapius was the legendary healer, later worshipped as a god of medicine. His sons serve the army as physicians.
Ajax, son of Telamon, was the greatest Greek warrior after Achilles. Achilles is withdrawn because Agamemnon took his prize.
Iris is the gods' messenger, often sent by Jove with commands to mortals; she is associated with the rainbow.
Aeneas is son of the goddess Venus and the mortal Anchises; he later becomes ancestor of the Romans in Virgil's epic.
The Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles, separating Europe from Asia.
Sarpedon and Glaucus are Trojan allies from Lycia in southern Asia Minor; Sarpedon is a son of Jove.

literary_notes.text: Jove is shown as deliberate and deceptive, using a lie to serve his own plan.
"Surely not to be accomplished" warns the reader that the dream's promise will fail.
The narrator tells us Agamemnon is wrong about Jove's plan, while Agamemnon still believes he will take Troy that day.
Dawn is a goddess who travels to Olympus to announce day, turning a daily event into divine action.
The narrator calls Agamemnon's counsel "cunning"; the plan is shaped by a deceptive dream and will go badly awry.
The proposed test of the army, with the order to stop any flight, hints at the chaos that follows when the men actually run.
Nestor's reasoning shows both his deference to rank and his prudence, presenting Agamemnon's status as the dream's guarantee.
The army pouring from camp is compared to swarming bees, conveying their number, restless movement and the clustering of the crowd.
Descriptive tags such as "shepherd of his people" and "mighty charioteer" give each owner a defining trait in the sceptre's genealogy.
The narrator and some leaders know the speech is a trick, while the crowd takes it literally, which sets up the rush to the ships.
Two comparisons, stormy waves and wind-bent corn, show the mass of men swayed as one by a single speech.
The remark that return would be "not fated" signals that the gods will intervene to prevent the departure.
"Not slack" understates the case: Minerva obeys eagerly and at once.
Ulysses' tactful, flattering speech to nobles shows his famed persuasiveness and sense of rank.
Ulysses' harsh words and blows to commoners contrast with his courtesy to chiefs, exposing the poem's hierarchical values.
The crowd's rush is compared to crashing surf, conveying its noise, force and the sudden reversal of the flight.
Thersites' ugliness is described in detail, and his twisted body suggests his twisted, disruptive character.
Thersites' complaint about Agamemnon's greed partly echoes Achilles' real grievance, yet the base speaker makes the criticism sound ugly.
The golden sceptre raising a bloody weal shows royal authority physically enforcing order against challenge.
The curt closing line lets the crowd's verdict stand as the narrator's final word, endorsing Ulysses' action.
Comparing the soldiers to children or widowed women is a sharp rebuke, implying they are helpless and unmanly in their complaints.
The screaming mother bird and her helpless young stir pity, making the serpent's cruelty vivid and the omen memorable.
Calchas's reading of the sparrows predicts the long war and eventual fall of Troy, turning the omen into a prophecy of the tenth year.
Waves battering a headland compare the surging, noisy rush of the army to the ships, giving it elemental force.
Jove's refusal hints that the Achaeans will suffer greatly, as he has promised Achilles.
The forest fire likens the glare of massed bronze armour to a blaze seen from far off.
Comparing Agamemnon to Jove, Mars and Neptune presents him as godlike in appearance and kingly in stature.
Ten tongues and a bronze heart exaggerate the impossibility of naming the whole army, stressing the Muses' knowledge.
Fixed descriptions such as "Thisbe the haunt of doves" and "Arne rich in vineyards" give each place a brief identity in the long list.
The small man with linen armour but unmatched spear skill is sketched in one quick contrast.
Agamemnon is shown as glorious and supreme, his power seen in his bronze armour and the number of his men.
The tale of a boastful mortal punished by the Muses warns against human pride before the gods.
Nireus is defined by contrast: great beauty but little strength or following, a quick sketch of a minor figure.
The line echoes sentence 232, stressing that the army's order survives its loss and sets up the theme of leadership.
The poet turns to address the Muse directly, asking for the knowledge to rank the best warriors and horses.
The mares are as fleet as birds, a compact image of their speed.
The marching army is compared to a consuming fire and to the quaking earth under Jove's wrath, conveying its vast, destructive power.
The goddess in disguise scolds Priam for treating war lightly, while she herself is deceiving the Trojans on Jove's orders.
The Greek host is compared to leaves and sand, conveying their overwhelming number.
The sons' disregard of their father's prophecy hints at their coming deaths, as fate lures them to destruction.
Comparing Nastes to a girl in gold mocks his vanity and shows the poem's scorn for unwarlike display.
